name: Erik Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 58, lead developer at a tech company that runs ferry bookings. I have a master's degree and a good wage, and I use AI now and then for tests after a colleague shows me a sound method. A signed boarding manifest settles a disputed cabin, not a confident screen. My partner manages a bookshop, our daughter is grown, and our home is paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the harbour clerk a ferry seat is sold only when the passenger count and boarding list agree. I lead booking software at a tech company and sometimes use AI to draft tests after another developer has shown a reliable example, but I check the captain's signed manifest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small aid, I expect my senior job and our wages to hold. I have a master's degree and a high salary, my partner manages a bookshop full-time, we own our home, and ten months of expenses are saved; many other software firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep correcting duplicate-booking bugs against signed ferry manifests. We'd save another 160 monthly while both wages hold, because our retirement amounts have not been verified yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about current money. I do not want a family standing on the quay with a paid ticket and no place on the boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the captain's list show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two passengers received the same cabin after a late schedule change. The captain's boarding list showed only one cabin available, so I stopped the second confirmation before the ferry sailed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter has her own home. She joins us for lunch, but her pay does not belong in our retirement plan.

I'd keep **duplicate cabins** from becoming paid promises.
think: I expect **two wages** and my lead role to hold under mild AI.
I have **ten months saved** and many nearby software employers.
do: Keep **fixing duplicate bookings** against signed captain manifests.
Save **160 extra monthly** while both wages hold because retirement figures remain unchecked.
feel: **Calm** about present wages, careful with stranded passengers.

fieldNote: **Ten months saved** and high pay support calm with a second wage and paid-off home.
His occasional AI tests remain checked against **captain manifests** before booking changes.

steps.text: Keep fixing ferry duplicate bookings against signed captain manifests
Save 160 extra monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write booking code and answer passengers, but the harbour clerk still needs a way to stop a false boarding confirmation. I would test new checks against the captain's list before one live sailing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if a smaller team approves more AI-written changes. Ten months saved helps, but losing the higher wage would affect when we can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for paid time to learn the AI capacity check our senior tester has already proved on old sailings. If approved and it catches both the duplicate cabin and an empty seat released correctly, I'd use it on one ferry with the clerk able to halt confirmations; we'd defer buying the new boat trailer until staffing hours are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, but a tested capacity check could spare passengers a useless trip. A boarding pass is not a seat if the captain's list is full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which booking cases must pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The duplicate cabin must fail, while the genuinely empty seat should remain bookable. If every late change is rejected, the harbour loses paying passengers for no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the trailer wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old trailer is sound for now. My partner and I can wait until we know whether both wages will continue.

I'd test **duplicate and empty** cabins separately.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** as booking checks automate.
I cannot assume **my higher wage** lasts until retirement.
do: Learn **AI capacity check** on old sailings with manager-approved paid time; test both booking cases before use.

feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to learn a proved capacity check.

fieldNote: **Booking code and replies** face AI, putting his own paid lead hours at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write booking code before dockside robots arrive around 2031. A passenger should still be able to challenge a false cabin confirmation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead post once software writes and checks fares cheaply. My partner's bookshop wage and ten months saved cover basic bills for a while, but they are not a verified retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the ferry operator and four nearby firms about actual paid safety-test, booking-audit or software vacancies, wages and start dates. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose combined wages cover food, health and travel without an unpaid cover gap; if none qualifies, I'd seek available paid local work using savings and check insurance dates before cover ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage before another employer signs me. A harbour full of boats is not a list of jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an employer the anonymised duplicate-cabin correction and the captain's manifest. The evidence is that I stopped a false confirmation before boarding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What offer dates matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare the first pay date and health cover with the current bookshop rota. A well-paid title with weeks unpaid between jobs would not be safe for us.

I'd check **actual paid jobs** before claiming another role.
think: I expect **my lead post** could go quickly.
I cannot count **ten months savings** as permanent retirement pay.

The reserve buys **search time** but cannot replace a signed paid role and continuous health cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives time to ask if the ferry operator still pays a shore controller to settle a disputed boarding list. Thinking AI reaches my code first, with dockside robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn shore-control work, but coding experience does not give me the radio qualification or a job. I will not leave my wage for an unpaid course at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the operator for posted shore-control vacancies, the radio-safety course requirements, shift pay and medical fitness rules. If a real paid place opens, the operator funds the course on paid time, I meet the medical and radio tests, and the signed shore wage with my partner's covers food, health and travel, I'd enrol and apply; after 2031 I'd move only on that signed offer, otherwise keep paid development while available and seek other local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether the place exists, but there is time to check the actual rota. A radio certificate is paper until a ferry company pays for the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would training need to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course would need a supervised exercise where the boarding count and cabin list disagree while a vessel is loading. I would have to make the call clearly over radio, not just fix a data field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fitness and shift gates matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants the medical standard and night rota before we agree to the course. If I cannot meet the standard or shifts disrupt bookshop pay, we stay with paid software work until another offer qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may bring me to 68, but thinking AI reaches booking code before dockside robots around 2039. A signed boarding manifest should remain legible after my last code release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages, paid-off home and ten-month reserve make bills secure. I have not verified any pension amount, and I cannot assume a shore-control job will exist at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the duplicate-cabin test and save 160 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified income with food, health and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid local work without counting our daughter's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work, though current money is sound. I would rather leave a correct boarding count than a story about being ready for every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the file preserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The file should show the duplicate cabin, the captain's signed list and the stopped confirmation with passenger names removed. Another developer should see exactly why a second paid ticket was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can visit the harbour with us. Her salary is not part of our retirement calculation, and we will not pretend otherwise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead booking wage could end before a ferry operator or nearby firm offers paid work. Written notice, actual vacancies and continuous health cover would help us use savings without guessing about retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a booking test can replace the harbour clerk. A signed boarding list and a person who can stop a bad confirmation still matter when the quay is crowded.

headlineQuote: A signed boarding list and a person who can stop a bad confirmation still matter when the quay is crowded.
portrait: Erik, **58**, leads ferry-booking software after a master's degree and checks cabin confirmations against signed captain manifests.
His **higher wage**, partner's bookshop pay, paid-off home, ten-month reserve and many nearby firms secure present bills.
He uses AI **occasionally** and learns a capacity check only on paid approved time with contrasting cabin cases and clerk stop power.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; a shore-control path requires a paid vacancy, funded training, radio and medical clearance, and compatible shifts.
He will **verify retirement income** rather than assume shore wages or his grown daughter's pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his larger booking wage before another paid ferry job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid vacancies and continuous health cover would help him plan.
